I can tell you from personal experience that pathological behaviors are encouraged in special ed. Not deliberately so (at least not by the teachers actually running the class), but students will act differently in special ed than they do outside of it. It's likely long term exposure to that environment will rub off on them. This may not be the case for every special ed class, but it's definitely been the case for what I've witnessed first hand.

Talk to anyone who's been dealing with children for a while, those who I've known will tell you they get more behavioral problems (and stranger ones) now than they used to. Why? There are a number of factors involved, divorce, drugs, prescription medication, changes in social structure...

I agree that gathering and properly interpreting statistical data is difficult, but this article sounds like it's trying to dismiss a problem rather than gather higher quality evidence and examine it more carefully.
I often wonder about that. Are there more, or are we just better at diagnosing them?

The diagnoses are incredibly sloppy. I was diagnosed with dyslexia. The institution which performed the test estimates 10% of the population is dyslexic. There is some dispute over whether dyslexia is over or under diagnosed, with estimates ranging from 2% to 25% of the population having it. The reading curriculum I was given was kept around a second grade level (they had us using books intended for much younger children for as long as I was kept in the special ed reading class). When my reading comprehension was assessed, I obtained the highest score possible, and I was the only student at that school to do so; this wasn't because I'd been indefinitely assigned to a second grade reading class. It is far from uncommon for children diagnosed with dyslexia to develop above average reading skills. And this isn't something that should be possible for someone with dyslexia.

ADD is even more abused. Drugging young children when they should be learning to control their behavior just doesn't sound like a good idea. Even assuming it provides the desired effects in the short term, I don't see how they could develop the way they're naturally supposed to while their brain is being screwed with. If you were to restrict someone to a wheelchair long term, their legs would atrophy and they'd have a harder time doing what they naturally could without the wheelchair. How are children supposed to develop natural impulse control when the impulses they need to learn to control are being suppressed with drugs? Take a look at Fontline's Medicating Kids to get an idea of how bad the drug industry is. Some of the side-effects they show are less severe than what I've witnessed first hand, but I can tell you from personal experience that they are criminally negligent in their diagnoses and treatment. The history of the lobotomy also sheds some light on how out of hand things can get.

There are different quality students. Some are self motivated, and try to resist distractions. Some are class clowns, and like to get away with whatever they can and cause as much disruption as possible. Most are in between, and they'll blend in with the dominant influence. By themselves they're OK, they listen, think, answer questions, and follow instructions. Pair them up with a disruptive student though, and they join in on the fun. The high quality students can have some influence too, and they reinforce each other.

But disruptive students tend to draw most of the attention. If their behavior is accepted, it sets a standard for everyone else. Why put in extra effort, if it gets you the same thing as someone who just doesn't give a fuck? Hell, if disruptive behavior is rewarded, why wouldn't you try to adopt it?
